DNS

Purpose:
Translates human-readable domain names (example.com) into IP addresses computers use to route traffic.

Architecture:
Hierarchical, distributed database: Root servers -> TLD servers (.com, .org) -> Authoritative name servers for the specific domain. Resolvers (often your ISP's or a public one like 8.8.8.8) cache results and query on your behalf.

Workflow:
1. App asks OS resolver for example.com.
2. Resolver checks its cache; if empty, asks a root server, which points to the .com TLD server.
3. TLD server points to example.com's authoritative server.
4. Authoritative server returns the IP (A/AAAA record).
5. Resolver caches it and returns it to the app.

Packet structure:
DNS messages are typically single UDP packets (port 53) containing a header plus question/answer/authority/additional sections.

Header fields:
Transaction ID, flags (query/response, recursion desired), question count, answer count, followed by the actual question and resource records.

Advantages:
Decouples human-friendly names from IPs that can change; caching makes it fast; hierarchical design scales globally.

Limitations:
Cache poisoning risk; propagation delay when records change (TTL-bound); plaintext by default (mitigated by DNSSEC/DoH/DoT).

Use cases:
Every domain name lookup - visiting a website, connecting to an API, sending email (via MX records), CDN routing (via geo-aware DNS).

Performance:
Low latency due to caching at multiple levels (browser, OS, resolver); TTL tuning trades off freshness vs. lookup speed.

Security:
DNSSEC adds cryptographic signing to prevent record tampering; DoH/DoT (DNS over HTTPS/TLS) encrypt queries to prevent eavesdropping.

Vulnerabilities:
Cache poisoning, DNS spoofing, DDoS against resolvers/authoritative servers, DNS tunneling (used for data exfiltration).

Troubleshooting:
`nslookup`/`dig`/`Resolve-DnsName` to query records directly; check TTLs; verify authoritative server delegation with `dig NS domain`.

Best practices:
Set sensible TTLs (short during migrations, longer once stable); enable DNSSEC where supported; use reputable/monitored resolvers.

Examples:
An A record maps example.com -> 93.184.216.34; an MX record tells mail servers where to deliver mail for a domain.

TLS SSL

Purpose:
Provides encryption, data integrity, and authentication for data in transit (SSL is the legacy predecessor to TLS, now considered insecure/deprecated).

Architecture:
Uses asymmetric cryptography (public/private key pairs, certificates) to establish a session, then switches to fast symmetric encryption for the actual data transfer. Certificates are issued/verified via a Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) and Certificate Authorities (CAs).

Workflow:
1. Client Hello (supported ciphers, TLS version).
2. Server Hello + certificate (public key).
3. Client verifies certificate against trusted CAs.
4. Key exchange establishes a shared symmetric session key (via Diffie-Hellman in modern TLS).
5. Both sides switch to encrypted communication using the session key.

Packet structure:
TLS records wrap application data; each record has a type (handshake, alert, application data), version, and length.

Header fields:
Not header-based like IP/TCP - structured as a record protocol with handshake sub-messages (ClientHello, ServerHello, Certificate, Finished).

Advantages:
Strong confidentiality and integrity guarantees; authenticates the server (and optionally the client); widely supported and standardized.

Limitations:
Adds handshake latency (mitigated by TLS 1.3's 1-RTT handshake and session resumption); certificate management overhead.

Use cases:
HTTPS, secure email (SMTPS/IMAPS), VPNs, secure API communication, any sensitive data in transit.

Performance:
TLS 1.3 significantly reduced handshake round trips vs 1.2; session resumption/0-RTT further reduces reconnect latency.

Security:
Core security building block for the internet; must disable weak ciphers/old versions (SSLv3, TLS 1.0/1.1 are deprecated).

Vulnerabilities:
Historical: Heartbleed, POODLE, BEAST - mostly tied to outdated versions/implementations; misconfigured/self-signed certs enabling MITM; expired certificates.

Troubleshooting:
`openssl s_client -connect host:443` to inspect the handshake/cert chain; browser padlock/cert details; check expiry and CA trust chain.

Best practices:
Use TLS 1.2 minimum (prefer 1.3), automate certificate renewal (e.g. Let's Encrypt/ACME), disable weak cipher suites, enforce HSTS.

Examples:
A browser padlock icon indicates a valid TLS certificate chain back to a trusted root CA for that domain.

OSI MODEL

Purpose:
A conceptual 7-layer framework for how network communication is organized, so each layer only needs to know about the layer directly above/below it.

Architecture:
1. Physical - raw bits over a medium (cables, radio).
2. Data Link - frames, MAC addressing, error detection on a local link (Ethernet, Wi-Fi).
3. Network - logical addressing and routing (IP, ICMP).
4. Transport - end-to-end delivery, reliability (TCP, UDP).
5. Session - manages sessions/connections between apps.
6. Presentation - data format/encoding, encryption, compression (TLS often modeled here).
7. Application - the protocols apps actually talk (HTTP, DNS, SMTP).

Workflow:
Data flows down the stack on the sender (each layer adds its own header - encapsulation), across the wire at the physical layer, then up the stack on the receiver (each layer strips its header - decapsulation).

Packet structure:
Not a single format - it's the layering model other protocols' packets/frames map onto.

Header fields:
N/A at this level; see individual protocols (Ethernet, IP, TCP).

Advantages:
Standard vocabulary for discussing networking; clean separation of concerns; easier troubleshooting (isolate which layer is failing).

Limitations:
Real-world stacks (TCP/IP) don't map cleanly onto all 7 layers; mostly a teaching/reference model rather than an implementation spec.

Use cases:
Teaching, troubleshooting methodology ('is this a Layer 2 or Layer 3 problem'), vendor documentation.

Performance:
N/A - conceptual model, not a runtime component.

Security:
Security controls exist at every layer (MAC filtering at L2, firewalls at L3/L4, TLS at L6, auth at L7).

Vulnerabilities:
N/A directly, but attacks are often described by the layer they target (e.g. ARP spoofing = L2, SYN flood = L4).

Troubleshooting:
Bottom-up approach: check physical link -> L2 connectivity (ARP/MAC) -> L3 (ping, routing) -> L4 (port reachability) -> L7 (application logs).

Best practices:
Use the model as a mental checklist when diagnosing 'why can't A reach B', not as literal code architecture.

Examples:
A browser request: HTTP (L7) -> TLS (L6) -> TCP (L4) -> IP (L3) -> Ethernet (L2) -> electrical signal (L1).

TCP

Purpose:
Connection-oriented, reliable transport protocol that guarantees ordered, error-checked delivery of a byte stream.

Architecture:
Uses a 3-way handshake to establish a connection, sequence/acknowledgment numbers to track delivery, and windowing for flow control.

Workflow:
1. SYN (client) -> SYN-ACK (server) -> ACK (client) establishes the connection.
2. Data is sent in segments, each acknowledged by the receiver; lost segments are retransmitted.
3. Connection closes via a FIN/ACK exchange (or RST for abrupt termination).

Packet structure:
TCP segment = header + data payload, carried inside an IP packet.

Header fields:
Source/Destination port, Sequence Number, Acknowledgment Number, Flags (SYN, ACK, FIN, RST), Window Size, Checksum.

Advantages:
Reliable, ordered delivery; built-in flow control and congestion control; widely supported by every OS/network device.

Limitations:
More overhead than UDP (handshake, acks, retransmission); head-of-line blocking can add latency for real-time use cases.

Use cases:
Web traffic (HTTP), email, file transfer, anything requiring guaranteed delivery and order.

Performance:
Congestion control algorithms (Cubic, BBR) adapt sending rate to network conditions; window scaling improves throughput on high-latency links.

Security:
TCP itself has no encryption - relies on TLS on top; vulnerable to SYN flood DoS attacks without protections like SYN cookies.

Vulnerabilities:
SYN flood attacks, TCP session hijacking, sequence number prediction attacks (mostly mitigated by modern randomization).

Troubleshooting:
`netstat`/`ss` to check connection states, Wireshark to inspect handshakes/retransmissions, checking for excessive retransmits indicating packet loss.

Best practices:
Tune keepalive/timeout settings for long-lived connections; use connection pooling in applications to avoid handshake overhead per request.

Examples:
Every HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 connection runs over TCP; SSH and most database connections use TCP too.

HTTP HTTPS

Purpose:
Application-layer protocol for transferring data on the web - the basis of virtually all browser/API traffic.

Architecture:
Request/response model over TCP (HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2) or UDP-based QUIC (HTTP/3). HTTPS = HTTP wrapped in TLS for encryption, integrity, and server authenticity.

Workflow:
Client sends a request (method, path, headers, optional body) -> server processes it -> server returns a response (status code, headers, body). For HTTPS, a TLS handshake happens first to establish an encrypted channel.

Packet structure:
Text-based (HTTP/1.1) or binary framed (HTTP/2, HTTP/3) messages carried inside TCP segments (or QUIC/UDP for HTTP/3).

Header fields:
Common headers: Host, Content-Type, Content-Length, Authorization, Cache-Control, Set-Cookie, User-Agent.

Advantages:
Simple, human-readable (v1.1), universally supported, stateless (easy to scale horizontally), rich ecosystem of tooling.

Limitations:
HTTP/1.1 has head-of-line blocking; stateless nature means session/auth state must be managed separately (cookies, tokens).

Use cases:
Web pages, REST APIs, webhooks, file downloads, virtually all client-server web communication.

Performance:
HTTP/2 multiplexes multiple requests over one connection (fixes head-of-line blocking at the app layer); HTTP/3/QUIC further reduces latency by avoiding TCP handshake overhead.

Security:
HTTPS (TLS) provides encryption, integrity, and server identity verification via certificates; HSTS forces HTTPS-only connections.

Vulnerabilities:
Man-in-the-middle attacks on plain HTTP, cross-site scripting (XSS), cross-site request forgery (CSRF), injection attacks via unvalidated input.

Troubleshooting:
Browser DevTools Network tab, `curl -v`, checking status codes (4xx = client error, 5xx = server error), verifying TLS cert validity.

Best practices:
Always use HTTPS in production; set proper cache headers; use meaningful status codes; validate/sanitize all input server-side.

Examples:
GET /api/users/42 returns a 200 with a JSON body; POST /login submits credentials in the request body over HTTPS.
